items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I heard about one that was playing in a district which was quite some distance from where we lived and that had a family of musicians working with them. The trumpet player was called Gabriel and I was told that he was very good.

ctx.x: Another one was: How do you feel to-night, Mr. Sampson? Mr. Sampson would say: Just like that woman's mouth, and point to some woman in the crowd. The other one who was usually known as the straight man would ask: How's that? and Sampson would say: wide open.

A group of these medicine shows would travel from city to city and play in different parts of the town and I heard about one that was playing in a district which was quite some distance from where we lived and that had a family of musicians working with them. The trumpet player was called Gabriel and I was told that he was very good. We had moved again and were now living on lower Carlisle Avenue, two blocks from where the red light district was. Red light district was the name for any district where prostitution…

One day I was playing in Sinton Park and I heard someone call another boy Gabriel and I was curious to know who this was because I have been told that I was a very fine trumpet player. He was playing baseball with some other boys and when I did get a good look at him, I saw that it was Sidney De Paris whom I had attended school with in Crawfordsville, Indiana and played the alto horn at church concerts.
